--- title: "Invasive vector species" description: "WHO Global database on invasive mosquito vector species. At present, the database contains data on detection of *Anopheles stephensi* outside of its native ecosystems." date: 10/23/2024 # mm-dd-yyyy image: "images/invasive_vector_species.png" categories: - Entomology - Country-level - Global - Annual - Surveillance / Routine --- ::: {.page-tabs .panel-tabset} ## Overview

About the data

The global database on invasive mosquito vector species was established in 2019 following the recommendations of the WHO's first Technical Consultation on the spread of *Anopheles stephensi*. The database is designed to allow tracking of the geographical spread of malaria vector species that pose a threat to malaria control and elimination efforts. The database aims to support the evaluation of risks posed by invasive vector species and to promote and inform prompt action to mitigate this risk. These datasets provide information on long term trends in distribution and spread of new or emerging mosquito vectors of malaria and enable tracking the spread of invasive vector species such as *Anopheles stephensi* comparison between countries. The data provided are on an annual time scale at the national level and would not be suitable for subnational analysis or to explore seasonal trends in malaria. Tracking surveillance activities helps to understand current research gaps. Knowledge of where studies are either being planned, currently underway, or recently completed, helps to inform where to direct resources for future studies.

Accessing the data

The data can be accessed via the WHO website through its Global Malaria Programme page on the [Malaria Threats Map](https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats/#/stories?theme=prevention). The data has a web page which includes useful contextual information as well as additional resources. The data can be viewed in the original report in excel format as it is usually preferable for modelling to have an excel spreadsheet. - To access the data, click on the [link](https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats) to access the [Malaria Threats Map](https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats/) page. - Click on the data download tile. - Select the theme `Invasive Vector Species` to access the `Invasive Vector Species` detections. - Data can be filtered according to `species` and `year` (1984-2024) in which collected. - Filter can be applied according to location. - Follow the prompts to select and download data. - The data is downloaded as an Excel file. The downloaded data can be plotted according to the geography for which the filters were selected (species, year collected and location). At this stage, dashboard summaries are not available for this thematic area.

What does the data look like?

Sometimes the data needs to be prepared before it is able to be plotted. ![Figure 1: Distribution of *Anopheles stephensi* in Kenya for 2022-2024.](images/distributionn_of_anopheles_stephensi_kenya.png){fig-align="left"} The distribution of *An. stephensi* was plotted for all districts in Kenya between 2022-2024. The method employed for collecting the specimens were recorded and the main methods of collection were the dipping method for mosquito larvae and the use of the light trap for collection of adult mosquitoes. The species identification was confirmed using molecular techniques. **Description** The data can be viewed as a spreadsheet, plotted on a map to show distribution or as a dashboard giving a summary of epidemiological and entomological data. The data can also be downloaded as Excel documents from the "Download Data" page. ![Figure 2: The occurrence of all invasive species from 2010 – 2024.](images/occurance_of_invasive_species.png){fig-align="left"} Figure 2 shows the distribution of all invasive mosquito species in Africa and south-east Asia for the past 14 years. It is apparent that *An. stephensi* is native to south-east Asia but it is an invasive species in north Africa. A number of sites were negative for *An. stephensi*. This information can be used for revising malaria control protocols. ![Figure 3: Sample of the summary dashboard that can be created using the distribution data.](images/summary_dashboard.png){fig-align="left"} Figure 3 shows a snap-shot of the summary data that can be generated from the selected dataset with the use of the appropriate filters. In this example, the vectors of Angola are listed and it is evident that *An. stephensi* has not yet moved down along the west coast of Africa. The insecticide resistance status of the vector mosquitoes is also given. The [complete dashboard](https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats/#/dashboards?country=AO&theme=prevention) provides more information.

Citing the data

Please acknowledge the use of these datasets by including the following reference in your publications: https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats/#/download. Include year, date of access, acknowledgement of the countries having provided the underlying data (in the event that the source refers to ministries of health or national malaria control programs of specific countries).

Examples of data use in literature

- WHO initiative to stop the spread of *Anopheles stephensi* in Africa. 2023 (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/372259/WHO-UCN-GMP-2023.06-eng.pdf?sequence=1). - Al-Eryani, S.M., Irish, S.R., Carter, T.E. et al. Public health impact of the spread of *Anopheles stephensi* in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region countries in Horn of Africa and Yemen: need for integrated vector surveillance and control. Malar J 22, 187 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12936-023-04545-y - Mnzava, A., Monroe, A.C. & Okumu, F. *Anopheles stephensi* in Africa requires a more integrated response. Malar J 21, 156 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12936-022-04197-4 - Abubakr M, Sami H, Mahdi I, Altahir O, Abdelbagi H, Mohamed NS, Ahmed A. The Phylodynamic and Spread of the Invasive Asian Malaria Vectors, *Anopheles stephensi*, in Sudan. Biology (Basel). 2022 Mar 7;11(3):409. doi: 10.3390/biology11030409. PMID: 35336783; PMCID: PMC8945054. - Ismail, R.B.Y., Bozorg-Omid, F., Osei, J.H.N. et al. Predicting the environmental suitability for *Anopheles stephensi* under the current conditions in Ghana. Sci Rep 14, 1116 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-51780-7 - Sinka ME, Pironon S, Massey NC, Longbottom J, Hemingway J, Moyes CL, WillisM KJ. - A new malaria vector in Africa: Predicting the expansion range of *Anopheles stephensi* and identifying the urban populations at risk. September 2020. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences DOI:10.1073/pnas.2003976117 - Kweka EJ. *Anopheles stephensi*: a guest to watch in urban Africa. Trop Dis Travel Med Vaccines. 2022 Apr 1;8(1):7. doi: 10.1186/s40794-022-00165-7. PMID: 35361266; PMCID: PMC8973991. ## Visualisations

How to use this data

The data contained in the database can be explored through the interactive data visualization platform [Malaria Threats Map](https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme/surveillance/malaria-threats-map). The platform provides a spreadsheet of the requested data in an Excel format. Distribution maps of the spread of invasive species can be generated from this data. A dashboard of malaria epidemiology and entomology can also be accessed via [this website](https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats/#/dashboards?country=AO).

How to plot this data

To access the specific data used in the visualisations: 1. Navigate to the [Malaria Threats Map page](https://apps.who.int/malaria/maps/threats/) 2. Below the right-most window labelled 'Data Download', click on the 'DOWNLOAD DATA' button. 3. Select the 'Invasive vector species' tile. 4. Select 'ADD TO DOWNLOAD'. 5. Select 'NEXT STEP'. Follow the prompts to download your files. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("theme_health_radar.R")) # source in the theme functions library(rdhs) library(ggrepel) library(sf) library(rnaturalearth) library(rnaturalearthdata) library(whowmr) library(dplyr) library(stringr) library(tidyr) library(forcats) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define the elimination 8 countries africa_names <- c("Burundi", "Ethiopia", "Mozambique", "Sudan", "Djibouti", "Ghana", "Kenya", "Eritrea", "Nigeria", "United Republic of Tanzania") # Read in the data, and filter our countries outside of Africa data <- readxl::read_xlsx("data/MTM_INVASIVE_VECTOR_SPECIES_20250109.xlsx", sheet = "Data") |> filter(COUNTRY_NAME %in% africa_names) ``` ::: Visualising the spread of sites at which invasive vector species were sampled can be effectively done using a map. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define a single colour for the plot single_color <- "#1b9e77" # Load the shapefile data for African countries and filter for specific countries africa <- ne_countries(continent = "Africa", returnclass = "sf") |> # Correct the name "eSwatini" to "Eswatini" mutate(name = if_else(name == "eSwatini", "Eswatini", name)) |> # Keep only the specified countries filter(name %in% c("Kenya", "Ethiopia", "Eritrea", "Djibouti", "Sudan")) # Convert LATITUDE and LONGITUDE columns to numeric data$LATITUDE <- as.numeric(data$LATITUDE) data$LONGITUDE <- as.numeric(data$LONGITUDE) # Filter the data for the specified countries and select relevant columns sites <- data |> filter(COUNTRY_NAME %in% c("Kenya", "Ethiopia", "Eritrea", "Djibouti", "Sudan")) |> select(COUNTRY_NAME, SITE_NAME, LATITUDE, LONGITUDE) # Create a ggplot object with the shapefile data ggplot(data = africa) + # Plot the shapefile data with grey borders geom_sf(color = "darkgrey", size = 0.3) + # Add points for the sites, coloured by the single color defined above geom_point(data = sites, aes(x = LONGITUDE, y = LATITUDE), colour = single_color, size = 2) + # Add text labels for the country names geom_sf_text(aes(label = sovereignt), color = "black", size = 3) + # Apply custom theme theme_health_radar() + # Customize the theme to remove the x- and y-axes and grid lines theme( plot.caption.position = "plot", axis.title.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.title.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank() ) + # Add labels and title to the plot labs( title = "Sites at which invasive vector species were sampled (2012-2024)", caption = str_wrap( "Sites in North-East African countries at which invasive vector species were collected from 2012 to 2024. Ethiopia appears to hold the highest number of sampling sites. Source: Malaria Threats Map Invasive Vector Species", width = 50)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: A line plot is used to visualise the total number of Invasive Vector Species study samples collected each year. Including points at each data point is important for communicating that this data was collected annually, not continuously, and that data is not available every year. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Filter the data to include only rows where YEAR_START is not NA data |> filter(is.na(YEAR_START) == FALSE) |> # Count the number of samples for each year count(year = YEAR_START) |> # Create a ggplot object with the counted data ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n)) + # Add a line plot to the chart, coloured by single_color geom_line(colour = single_color) + # Add points to the plot, coloured by single_color geom_point(colour = single_color) + # Apply custom theme theme_health_radar() + # Customise the x-axis to show yearly breaks scale_x_continuous(breaks = min(data$YEAR_START):max(data$YEAR_START)) + # Add labels and title to the plot labs( x = "Year", y = "Number of samples", title = "Annual total number of samples collected per year", caption = str_wrap("The annual total number of samples of any species collected in Africa during Invasive Vector Species studies which began in each year. No studies began in the years 2015 or 2017. There appears to be an increase in the number of samples collected between 2014 and 2022, followed by a drop in 2023. Source: Malaria Threats Map Invasive Vector Species", width = 105)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Lastly, we look at the total number of Invasive Vector Species study samples collected in each country, rather than in each year. As the x-variable is categorical and not continuous, a bar plot is used. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define a single color for the bars single_color <- "#1b9e77" # Modify the COUNTRY_NAME to replace "United Republic of Tanzania" with "Tanzania" data |> mutate(COUNTRY_NAME = ifelse(COUNTRY_NAME == "United Republic of Tanzania", "Tanzania", COUNTRY_NAME)) |> # Count the number of samples for each country count(COUNTRY_NAME) |> # Create a ggplot object with the counted data ggplot(aes(x = COUNTRY_NAME, y = n)) + # Add bar plots to the chart, filled with the single colour geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = single_color) + # Apply custom theme theme_health_radar() + # Customize the x-axis text to be angled and adjusted theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 0.4)) + # Add labels and title to the plot labs( x = "", y = "Number of samples", title = "Total number of samples collected in each African country", caption = str_wrap("The total number of samples of any species collected in each African country during Invasive Vector Species studies. No samples were taken in countries not present on the plot. Over three times the number of samples were collected in Ethiopia than in the second most prolific country, Kenya. Source: Malaria Threats Map Invasive Vector Species", width = 100)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Modelling

How can this data be used in disease modelling?

::: {.cell} ::: Data on invasive mosquito vector species can be used in a range of malaria modelling applications: - To project the spread of disease if transmission efficiency of the invasive vector differs to the native vector, or their combined effects can inform the overall vectorial capacity in a given context. - When used in conjunction with other data sources such as climate projections, land cover or population density data, the location of the invasive species collected can be used to model population dynamics, as done by [Da Re, D. et al. (2022](https://parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13071-022-05414-4)) in their exploration of invasive *Aedes* species. This can further inform spatial risk mapping and/or be used to forecast further invasions of the species. These findings can also be used as inputs for models that evaluate intervention impact, as far as targeted vector control and changes in their effectiveness due to the presence of invasive species. ### Preparing the data We use the Ghana extract of the invasive vector species database. Anopheles stephensi was first confirmed in Ghana in 2022. Each row is one collection at one site. The `INVASIVE_STATUS` column tells us whether An. stephensi was found there. The records in this Ghana database are the kind of evidence a control programme has at the very start of an invasion: a short list of places that were searched, and a shorter list of places where something was found. That is not much, but it is enough to ask four practical questions, and this page works through each of them with a small, deliberately transparent model. The questions are: *how much extra malaria could this mosquito cause?*, *when in the year will it be around?*, *where should we look next?*, and *will our current control tools still work?* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ghana <- read_excel("data/GHANA_INVASIVE_VECTOR_SPECIES.xlsx", sheet = "Data") |> transmute( site = SITE_NAME, region = str_replace(ADMIN1, "Greater Accra Region", "Greater Accra"), latitude = LATITUDE, longitude = LONGITUDE, year = YEAR_START, month = MONTH_START, habitat = na_if(BREEDING_HABITAT, "Not available"), found = INVASIVE_STATUS == "Invasive" ) ghana |> filter(found) |> select(site, region, year, month, habitat) |> knitr::kable(caption = "The three Ghanaian sites where An. stephensi was confirmed.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: The three Ghanaian sites where An. stephensi was confirmed. |site |region | year|month |habitat | |:--------|:-------------|----:|:--------|:------------| |Dansoman |Greater Accra | 2022|June |Puddle | |Tuba |Greater Accra | 2022|February |Dug-out well | |Nima |Greater Accra | 2022|January |NA | ::: ::: The species was found at 3 of 18 sites searched, so this is a very early invasion. The useful models here are about anticipation, not about explaining an epidemic that has already happened. Every collection used the dipping method, meaning larvae were scooped from water; nobody was catching adults, so the database tells us where the mosquito breeds, not how many are flying or whom they bite. And the two sites with a recorded habitat are a puddle and a dug-out well, one natural and rain-fed, one man-made and permanent. ### How much extra malaria could this mosquito cause? Malaria modellers use one quantity to summarise how much transmission a mosquito population generates, called **vectorial capacity**. In words, it is: if one person is infectious today, how many new infectious bites will eventually come out of the mosquitoes that bite them? It depends on four things: $$\text{capacity} \;=\; \frac{(\text{how many mosquitoes per person}) \times (\text{how often it bites people})^2 \times (\text{chance it lives long enough})}{\text{daily death rate}}$$ The square on the biting term is the important part. A mosquito has to bite twice to pass on malaria — once to pick the parasite up, once to pass it on — so halving how often it feeds on people cuts transmission by three quarters, not by half. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # One function, four inputs. m = mosquitoes per person, a = bites on people per day, # mu = daily chance of dying, n = days the parasite needs to develop inside the mosquito. capacity <- function(m, a, mu, n) m * a^2 * exp(-mu * n) / mu # Typical values from the literature. An. stephensi feeds on cattle and other animals # far more readily than An. gambiae does, so it bites people less often. vectors <- tribble( ~species, ~bites_people_per_day, ~daily_death_rate, ~parasite_days, "An. gambiae s.l.", 0.30, 0.123, 11, "An. stephensi", 0.15, 0.155, 11 ) |> mutate(capacity_per_mosquito = capacity(1, bites_people_per_day, daily_death_rate, parasite_days)) vectors |> knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Species", "Bites on people per day", "Daily death rate", "Days for parasite to develop", "Capacity per mosquito"), caption = "Transmission capacity of a single mosquito of each species.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Transmission capacity of a single mosquito of each species. |Species | Bites on people per day| Daily death rate| Days for parasite to develop| Capacity per mosquito| |:----------------|-----------------------:|----------------:|----------------------------:|---------------------:| |An. gambiae s.l. | 0.30| 0.123| 11| 0.189| |An. stephensi | 0.15| 0.155| 11| 0.026| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ratio <- vectors$capacity_per_mosquito[1] / vectors$capacity_per_mosquito[2] # How much total transmission increases as An. stephensi builds up, relative to # the mosquitoes already present tibble(relative_numbers = seq(0, 12, by = 0.1)) |> mutate( native = vectors$capacity_per_mosquito[1], added = relative_numbers * vectors$capacity_per_mosquito[2], increase = added / native ) |> ggplot(aes(x = relative_numbers, y = increase)) + geom_line(colour = "#1b9e77") + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") + theme_health_radar() + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + labs( x = "An. stephensi per native mosquito", y = "Increase in malaria transmission", title = "How many An. stephensi would it take to double transmission?", caption = str_wrap("Because An. stephensi bites people less often than An. gambiae s.l., each individual contributes roughly a seventh as much transmission. It would take about seven of them per native mosquito to double transmission, shown by the dashed line.")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: So a single An. stephensi is not especially dangerous. Roughly 7.2 of them are needed to match one An. gambiae. The concern is not the individual mosquito but the number of them a city can support, and that brings us to where they breed. ### When in the year will it be around? Ghana's existing malaria mosquitoes breed in rain-filled ground pools, so their numbers rise and fall with the rains and crash in the dry season. A mosquito that also breeds in wells, tanks and stored water is not tied to the rain in the same way. The Ghana data hints at exactly this. The puddle detection at Dansoman was in **June and July**, at the height of the rains. The dug-out well detection at Tuba was in **February**, which is the dry season. Below is the simplest model that can express that difference: each month, the mosquito population grows towards whatever the available water can support that month. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Long-term average monthly rainfall for Accra (mm). accra_rain <- c(15, 33, 56, 81, 142, 178, 46, 15, 36, 64, 36, 23) rain_index <- accra_rain / max(accra_rain) months <- rep(1:12, times = 3) # simulate three years so the pattern settles # Two kinds of breeding habitat habitat_capacity <- tibble( step = seq_along(months), month = months, `Rain-filled puddles only` = 1000 * pmax(0.02, rain_index[months]), `Puddles plus wells and tanks` = 1000 * (0.60 + 0.40 * rain_index[months]) ) # One line of population growth: grow towards what this month's habitat can hold grow <- function(capacity, growth_rate = 1.2, start = 50) { n <- numeric(length(capacity)) n[1] <- start for (t in 2:length(capacity)) { n[t] <- n[t - 1] * exp(growth_rate * (1 - n[t - 1] / capacity[t])) } n } mosquitoes <- habitat_capacity |> mutate(across(c(`Rain-filled puddles only`, `Puddles plus wells and tanks`), grow)) |> filter(step > 24) |> # keep the final year mutate(month = factor(month.abb[month], levels = month.abb)) |> pivot_longer(cols = contains("s"), names_to = "habitat", values_to = "mosquitoes") mosquitoes |> ggplot(aes(x = month, y = mosquitoes, colour = habitat, group = habitat)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + theme_health_radar() + scale_colour_manual_health_radar() + labs( x = "", y = "Relative number of mosquitoes", colour = "", title = "Breeding habitat sets the season's length", caption = str_wrap("Mosquitoes that depend on rain-filled puddles almost disappear between December and March. Mosquitoes that can also use wells, tanks and stored water stay abundant all year.")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: This matters more than the size of the peak. Where transmission stops for a few months each year, chains of infection break and have to be re-started. Where it does not stop, they do not. A modest number of mosquitoes present in February can therefore do more damage than a large number present only in June. ### Where should we look next? Fifteen Ghanaian sites came back negative. Some of them are a few hundred metres from a positive site and some are thirty kilometres away, and those two situations do not deserve the same confidence. A simple screening rule captures this: risk falls off with distance from the nearest confirmed detection. Mosquito flight is short-range, so we use a few kilometres as the scale. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Approximate distance in km. Over an area this small, flat geometry is fine. distance_km <- function(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) { sqrt(((lat1 - lat2) * 111)^2 + ((lon1 - lon2) * 111 * cos(5.6 * pi / 180))^2) } # Ensure coordinates are numeric ghana <- ghana |> mutate( latitude = as.numeric(latitude), longitude = as.numeric(longitude)) positives <- ghana |> filter(found) |> mutate( latitude = as.numeric(latitude), longitude = as.numeric(longitude)) ghana_risk <- ghana |> rowwise() |> mutate( km_to_nearest = if (nrow(positives) > 0) { min(distance_km( latitude, longitude, positives$latitude, positives$longitude ), na.rm = TRUE) } else { NA_real_ }, risk = ifelse( is.na(km_to_nearest), NA_real_, exp(-km_to_nearest / 5) ) ) |> ungroup() ghana_risk |> ggplot(aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) + geom_point( aes( size = risk, colour = if_else(found, "Found", "Searched, not found") ), alpha = 0.85 ) + geom_text_repel( aes(label = site), size = 3.5, colour = "grey30", seed = 42, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.4 ) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) + coord_quickmap() + theme_health_radar() + scale_colour_manual_health_radar() + labs( x = "", y = "", colour = "", size = "Estimated risk", title = "Where An. stephensi is most likely to turn up next", caption = str_wrap( "Each point is a site in the Ghana database, sized by how close it is to a confirmed detection. This is a screening rule, not a distribution model: it says where to send the next survey team, and says nothing about whether the habitat there is suitable.")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ghana_risk |> filter(!found) |> slice_max(risk, n = 5) |> select(site, region, km_to_nearest, risk) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Site", "Region", "Km to nearest detection", "Estimated risk"), caption = "Negative sites closest to a confirmed detection - the first places to search again.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Negative sites closest to a confirmed detection - the first places to search again. |Site |Region | Km to nearest detection| Estimated risk| |:----------|:-------------|-----------------------:|--------------:| |Cantonment |Greater Accra | 2.63| 0.59| |Chorkor |Greater Accra | 3.02| 0.55| |Dzorwulu |Greater Accra | 3.49| 0.50| |East Legon |Greater Accra | 7.42| 0.23| |Sowutoum |Greater Accra | 9.40| 0.15| ::: ::: ### Will our current control tools still work? Bed nets and indoor spraying work by meeting mosquitoes that come into houses and bite people who are in bed. An. stephensi bites earlier in the evening and more often outdoors, so a smaller share of its bites can be intercepted this way. We can put that into the same capacity calculation by adjusting two numbers: it bites fewer people, and it is more likely to die doing so. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # phi = share of bites taken on people who are in bed; nets only reach those bites vectors_itn <- vectors |> mutate( share_of_bites_in_bed = c(0.85, 0.40), coverage = 0.70, # 70% of people sleeping under a net repelled = 0.56, killed = 0.41, # effect of a net on a mosquito that meets one bites_with_nets = bites_people_per_day * (1 - share_of_bites_in_bed * coverage * (repelled + killed)), deaths_with_nets = daily_death_rate + (1/3) * share_of_bites_in_bed * coverage * killed, capacity_with_nets = capacity(1, bites_with_nets, deaths_with_nets, parasite_days), `Bed nets alone` = 1 - capacity_with_nets / capacity_per_mosquito, `Larval control alone` = 0.50, # halving breeding sites halves mosquito numbers `Both together` = 1 - (1 - `Bed nets alone`) * (1 - `Larval control alone`) ) vectors_itn |> select(species, `Bed nets alone`, `Larval control alone`, `Both together`) |> pivot_longer(-species, names_to = "approach", values_to = "reduction") |> mutate(approach = fct_inorder(approach)) |> ggplot(aes(x = approach, y = reduction, fill = species)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) + theme_health_radar() + scale_fill_manual_health_radar() + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) + labs( x = "", y = "Reduction in transmission", fill = "", title = "Bed nets do less against a mosquito that bites outdoors", caption = str_wrap("At 70% net coverage, nets remove most of the transmission generated by An. gambiae s.l. but considerably less of that generated by An. stephensi, because fewer of its bites are taken on people in bed. Removing breeding sites closes the gap. The Ghana database is useful here in a very practical way: it names the habitats to target, in this case puddles and dug-out wells.")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The encouraging half of this result is that larval control, which is difficult against thousands of scattered rain pools, becomes realistic when the breeding sites are wells and stored water that people can point to. The database is, in effect, the beginning of that target list. ### Model assumptions Every number above rests on assumptions, and being clear about them is what separates a useful illustration from a misleading one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tribble( ~Assumption, ~`Why it matters`, "A 'not found' record means the mosquito was absent", "Larval dipping misses breeding sites. If the two species share breeding sites instead of having unlimited separate habitat, *An. stephensi* establishing should come partly at the native mosquito's expense, rather than being a clean addition on top. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # A simple two-species competition model: both species draw down the SAME # shared breeding capacity, rather than each having unlimited separate habitat. # alpha controls how much they compete for it: 0 means no competition (matching # the "simply adds" assumption), 1 means full competition, as if one species. alpha <- 0.3 # partial overlap - stephensi favours containers, gambiae favours puddles, but both use some of each K_native <- 1 # native capacity, normalised (matches section 1) stephensi_ratio <- vectors$capacity_per_mosquito[2] / vectors$capacity_per_mosquito[1] # ~0.14, from section 1 competition_step <- function(state, K1, K2, alpha, r = 0.3) { N1 <- state[["N1"]]; N2 <- state[["N2"]] c( N1 = N1 + r * N1 * (1 - (N1 + alpha * N2) / K1), N2 = N2 + r * N2 * (1 - (N2 + alpha * N1) / K2) ) } competition_result <- function(K2) { states <- accumulate(1:300, ~ competition_step(.x, K1 = K_native, K2 = K2, alpha = alpha), .init = c(N1 = 0.1, N2 = 0.1)) tail(states, 1)[[1]] } tibble(relative_numbers = seq(0, 12, by = 1)) |> mutate( K2 = relative_numbers * stephensi_ratio, result = map(K2, competition_result), N1 = map_dbl(result, "N1"), N2 = map_dbl(result, "N2"), `Simply adds (independent habitat)` = K_native + K2, `Shares breeding habitat` = N1 + N2 ) |> pivot_longer(c(`Simply adds (independent habitat)`, `Shares breeding habitat`), names_to = "assumption", values_to = "total_capacity") |> ggplot(aes(x = relative_numbers, y = total_capacity, colour = assumption)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + theme_health_radar() + scale_colour_manual_health_radar() + labs(x = "*An. stephensi* per native mosquito", y = "Total transmission capacity", colour = "", title = "What sharing breeding habitat changes", caption = str_wrap("The 'simply adds' line matches section 1's chart exactly. Once the two species compete for the same limited breeding sites, An. stephensi's gains come partly at the native mosquito's expense, so the true combined total grows more slowly - and at low relative densities, it may struggle to establish against an already-entrenched native population at all. Source: Model output.", width = 105)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](invasive_vector_species_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The gap between the two lines is the cost of the additive assumption: real breeding-site competition would make *An. stephensi*'s impact grow more slowly than section 1 suggests - though probably not as slowly as full competition would imply, since the two species don't rely on exactly the same habitats. ### Policy implications Three positive sites do not yet constitute an epidemic, so the decision facing Ghana is whether to act while quantities are still small, and that is a decision that has to be made before the evidence becomes obvious. If a single dipping survey finds the mosquito only half the time when it is genuinely present, then a "not found" result is weak evidence of absence. The practical conclusion is that one negative survey at a high-risk site should not close the file on it. Repeat visits, and collecting adults as well as larvae, are worth more than widening the search. The February detection in a dug-out well is the single most informative record in the dataset. If An. stephensi can carry a population through Accra's dry months in stored and standing water, the consequence is a longer transmission season rather than a higher peak - and surveillance timed to the rains would miss precisely the months that matter. Bed nets remain the foundation, but this exercise shows they do less work against a mosquito biting outdoors and early. Targeting breeding sites is the complement, and it is unusually feasible here because the habitats are man-made and locatable. That draws in water, housing and municipal authorities alongside the malaria programme. There is no measurement of how many An. stephensi there are, how often they bite people in Accra, or whether they carry parasites. Those three measurements would do more to sharpen every figure on this page than any amount of additional modelling, and collecting adult mosquitoes rather than only larvae is the first step toward them. :::
